name: Tara Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm training to be a primary school teacher, so it's lectures on child development and maths teaching, plus a school visit every Thursday where I help in a Year 2 class. I live at home with my mum and my nan in a terraced house, and I work Friday evenings and all day Saturday on the checkouts at the big supermarket. I get up at six most days. It's a lot, but I wanted this since I was about nine, when my own teacher, Mrs Pickering, stayed behind to help me read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, and I'd feel a bit smug. At work I'd say the self-checkouts are fine for a basket but people still queue at mine. With friends I'd say a teacher is a teacher and that children need a person at the front of the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I still worry, but about the usual things. Teaching jobs near us are few, and the schools say they've no money. I've got a loan and I'm on minimum wage. So even if AI is hype, whether I get a job in 2029 depends on the budget, not on computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my Saturday job, and I'd put aside about thirty pounds a month for the teaching exams I'll have to pay for. I'd ask the school I visit whether they take on student helpers in the holidays. I wouldn't start using AI, since I can do my lesson plans by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, steady. Not cheerful, but not scared. Just the same ordinary pressure I'm under now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if your Saturday hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum earns about the same as me from her care-home job, and Nan has her pension. We'd manage, but I'd be the one who stops buying anything. I'd skip the bus fare and walk to the supermarket, which is forty minutes, because I'd rather lose the sleep than the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't start using AI. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't see the point. I like writing my plans out, and I think children can tell when something's been copied. A mate on my course uses it for everything and her plans all sound the same. I'd rather be slow and mine.

say: Children need a **person** at the front of the class.
Self-checkouts are fine for a basket, but people still queue at my till.
think: Whether I get a job in 2029 depends on the school **budget**, not on computers.
I have a loan and minimum wage, so the usual worries stay.
do: Keep the Saturday **job** and put thirty pounds a month aside for exams.
Ask the school I visit about holiday helper work.
Keep writing my lesson plans by hand.
feel: Steady but not cheerful, under the same **ordinary** pressure as now.
S0.quote: Whether I get a job in 2029 depends on the budget, not on computers.
fieldNote: Tara's fear is the **school budget** and the few local teaching jobs, not technology.
She declines AI on principle: she thinks children can tell when a plan is copied.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday checkout shifts through the year
Put thirty pounds a month aside for the teaching exams
Ask the school about paid holiday helper work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be strange but teachers will still be needed. At work I'd say the supermarket already cut four of us last spring when the self-checkouts went in, so I know what's coming. I'd tell people to be kind to anyone whose job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be more worried about my Saturday job than my degree. Checkouts, orders and customer calls are what they move to software first. Teaching has the marking and admin that AI could do, so schools might hire fewer teaching assistants and ask teachers to do more. That's a squeeze I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my tutor and ask how the schools around here use these tools, because I'd rather hear it from someone I trust than from the internet. I'd look for a second weekend job, maybe in a care home like Mum's, where there's no software replacing a person. And I'd save, though not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd say I can see the edge of it. I'm not frightened for the teaching, but for the money that holds me up while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the self-checkouts came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager held a meeting and said nobody would be sacked. Then he just didn't replace the ones who left. My friend Gemma was on the tills for six years and her hours got cut to eight a week. She quit and now she's cleaning offices at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tools if your tutor said schools use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the school says I have to, then yes, but I'd want to be shown, step by step, and be told which bits I'm allowed to use. I wouldn't go and try it on my own first.

say: It will be strange, but **teachers** will still be needed.
The supermarket already cut four of us when the self-checkouts came in.
Be kind to anyone whose job goes.
think: I'm more worried about my Saturday **job** than my degree, as the checkouts go to software first.
Schools could hire fewer teaching assistants and ask teachers to do more.
do: Ask my **tutor** how local schools use these tools.
Look for a second weekend job in a care home like Mum's.
Save what I can, though not much.
feel: **Anxious**, not for the teaching but for the money that holds me up while I train.
S1.quote: The manager held a meeting and said nobody would be sacked. Then he just didn't replace the ones who left.
fieldNote: Tara has seen the **self-checkout** cut in her own shop and uses it as evidence of what comes.
She would only use AI if shown step by step by a trusted tutor, never alone.

steps.text: Ask my tutor how local schools use these tools
Look for a second weekend job at a care home
Learn the tools only when the school shows me step by step

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast. Two years is nothing. My nan says she's seen a lot of changes but never one that hits that quick. At work we'd be in a state, and nobody at head office would tell us anything until it's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really frightened. I'm only just finishing first year, and by the time I'm qualified in 2029, there might not be a school job for me. Mum's care home work might last, but the supermarket would go quickly, and then there's no money for the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the course because I don't know what else I'd do. I'd ask Mum and Nan if we can pool money, and I'd pick up as many care-home shifts as I could, since it's hands-on. I'd also go to the student support office and ask what happens if a course closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed. I'd feel sick every time I read the news, and I'd keep checking my phone for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum I'm sorry, because I'd feel I'd chosen the wrong thing. She'd tell me not to be daft and that I'm doing what I love. But I'd lie awake knowing Mum is cutting back on her own heating so I can finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would be different to a longer one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not trust any plan. With two years I can't change course, and I can't save enough. So I'd mostly be waiting to be told what to do, which I know is not a great answer.

say: Two years is too **fast**, and nobody at head office would tell us anything.
My nan has seen many changes but never one this quick.
think: By the time I'm **qualified**, there might not be a school job for me.
The supermarket would go quickly and the loan would still need paying.
do: Keep on with the course and pick up more **care-home** shifts.
Pool money with Mum and Nan.
Ask student support what happens if a course closes.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick when I read the news, checking my phone all the time.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake knowing Mum is cutting back on her own heating so I can finish.
fieldNote: Tara's panic is about the family: she knows her mum would cut her own **heating** so she can finish.
She admits she would mostly wait to be told what to do, because there is no time to change course.

steps.text: Stay on the teaching course and keep going to school visits
Ask student support what happens if the course closes
Take extra care-home shifts at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't nothing. I'd tell friends that if you're going to be a teacher you should still go for it, because children need a human in the room. At work I'd say don't panic, but also don't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I'd be anxious, but I'd feel I could get through it. I'd be qualified in 2029 with a couple of years of teaching before the robots would reach classrooms. Primary teaching is very hands-on, with the tying shoelaces and the crying, and I'd hope that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my course, apply to schools in our town and the next one over, and save a bit each month. I'd ask my tutor to show me how teachers use the tools, since I'd have time to learn them slowly. I'd keep my supermarket shifts until I qualify, even if they're reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not overwhelmed. I can look at five years and see where I'd be. It's the loan that nags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd learn slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to use it to cut down the marking, like making a spelling test or a worksheet. I'd learn that once I'm on placement and can see how a real teacher does it. Then I'd make up my own mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel to be in a classroom while this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd feel proud, honestly. If the world's changing, then the children need someone steady. And I'd be the person who can read a room, notice a child who's gone quiet, which no program does.

say: Five years isn't **nothing**, and children still need a human in the room.
Don't panic, but don't ignore it either.
think: I'd be anxious but could get through it, with two years of **teaching** before robots reach classrooms.
Primary teaching is hands-on, with shoelaces and crying.
do: Finish the course and apply to schools in our town and the **next** one over.
Save a bit each month and keep my supermarket shifts until I qualify.
Learn the tools slowly from a teacher on placement.
feel: Anxious but not **overwhelmed**, because I can look at five years and see where I'd be.
S3.quote: I'd be the person who can read a room, notice a child who's gone quiet, which no program does.
fieldNote: With five years, Tara moves from waiting to a **plan**: finish, apply widely, learn the tools on placement.
She finds pride in the human side of teaching, which she says no program does.

steps.text: Finish the course and apply to schools in two towns
Save a bit each month from the Saturday wage
Learn to make worksheets with the tools on placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and I probably wouldn't worry much at first. I'd say I'll do what I'm doing: get qualified, get a job, buy a little house one day. I'd tell friends who aren't sure what to study to pick something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit less anxious, but not calm. The thing I'd think about is what the world looks like when I'm 29 and trying to start a family. Ten years is enough to get a mortgage sorted, but not if the money changes. I'd still keep some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, get a school job, and try to pay down the loan. I'd learn the tools once schools start using them, not before. I'd probably help Mum and Nan with the house, because they've nobody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. I'd think about it now and then, like a rainy day that might come. It'd sit in the back of my mind and not stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your nan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nan would say it'll all sort itself out, and she'd probably be right about the bits that matter. I'd tell her I'll look after her, and she'd say she doesn't need looking after. We'd both be lying a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If ten years were too long to be useful, what's the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get comfortable and not prepare. People like me, who don't use the new stuff, would be last to learn it. I'd set a rule to try one new thing a year, even if I don't like it.

say: Ten years is long, so I'd just carry on, qualify and get a **job**.
Pick something with people in it.
think: I'd be less anxious but not calm, because I would be 29 and maybe starting a **family**.
I'd keep some savings, even in a long timeline.
do: Finish training, get a school job and pay down the **loan**.
Learn the tools once schools start using them.
Help Mum and Nan with the house.
feel: Mostly okay, like a rainy day that might **come** but doesn't stop me sleeping.
S4.quote: I'd set a rule to try one new thing a year, even if I don't like it.
fieldNote: Tara's concern becomes **comfort**: with ten years she thinks she'll get lazy about learning new things.
She sets herself a rule to try one new thing a year.

steps.text: Finish training and get a primary school job
Pay down the loan and keep some savings
Help Mum and Nan with the house costs
Try one new school tool each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, definitely. That's the one where I'd have no time and no money to change anything. It would help to know early what schools will actually do, to have someone at uni say honestly what's safe, and for the government to protect jobs like care and teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me, who aren't into technology, get written off. We're not stupid. We just want someone to show us what it is before we're told we're behind.

headlineQuote: We're not stupid. We just want someone to show us what it is before we're told we're behind.
portrait: Tara is a 19-year-old **primary teaching** student who lives with her mum and nan and works checkouts at a supermarket.
She is centre and resistant: she doesn't use AI, writes her plans by hand and trusts people she knows.
She has watched self-checkouts cut hours in her own shop, so she believes the warnings.
Her worry is the family's money and the few teaching jobs nearby, more than the technology.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because there would be no time or money to change anything.
whatWouldHelp: Honest early **information** from her university about what is safe, and someone to show her the tools first.
